project: A restaurant waitlist: parties quoted a wait, seated by size, tables turning over all evening.

steps.title: The floor, as something you can look at
steps.scene: Kothari's has twenty-two tables across three sections. The only place that knows which are free is a wipe-clean board behind the host stand, and it is wrong for about ten minutes after every departure.
steps.build: Load tables, sizes and sections once before the server listens, from `@ConfigurationProperties`, and serve a floor that can be filtered by section and by state — where free is derived from what is seated at the table, never stored as a flag somebody has to remember to clear.
steps.follows: Nothing can be quoted, seated or cleared until the floor exists.

story.want: see every table with its size, section and whether it is occupied
story.so: I can find a table without walking the floor

steps.summary: The app starts with 22 tables in three sections loaded once, and answers a floor filterable by section and state.

codes: no such table in this branch

data: tables(id, branch_id, no, seats 2|4|6, section, current_seating_id nullable, cleared_at nullable) — 10 two-tops, 8 four-tops, 4 six-tops
seed file seed/tables.csv read once at start-up
rules: State is derived on read from the table's current seating: `seated` while that seating has no leftAt; `uncleared` once the party has left and nobody has cleared the table (the seating stays current until the clear); `free` when no seating is current. No stored state flag.
Seeding runs before the first request and is idempotent — a second start does not duplicate tables.
Settings (database path, host, port, default quote minutes) come from one settings object; nothing hard-coded.
Filter values outside the enum are 400, not an empty list.
Filters are typed `@RequestParam` parameters bound to enums (an unknown value is 400); every response is a record DTO, never an entity; settings are one `@ConfigurationProperties` record.
ac_user: she sees 22 tables — ten twos, eight fours, four sixes — every one free
she sees only Garden tables and the count of free ones
ac_api: tables has 22 rows after both starts
only that table, with partyId and seatedMinutes
done: Both endpoints, both filters, both refusals.
Idempotent seeding covered by a test that starts twice.
No stored state column on tables.
The floor screen renders from these endpoints only.

try.do: Use the section and state selects. Count the tables: ten two-tops, eight four-tops, four six-tops. Then open `/branches/Baner/tables?section=Roof` in the browser.
try.see: 22 tables, every one free; the count line (shown · free, counted over the filtered tables) comes from GET /branches/Baner/tables, whose `section` and `state` filters are enum `@RequestParam`s. `section=Roof` is a 400 /errors/validation ProblemDetail, not an empty list. The floor was seeded by a bean before Tomcat started listening, and there is no `state` column anywhere — a table is seated when a seating is open on it, uncleared when the party has left and nobody has wiped it, free otherwise.

steps.title: A party joins the list
steps.scene: The Kulkarnis arrive: six people, one name, no reservation. Meera writes 'Kulkarni 6' on the board and hopes she can read it in an hour.
steps.build: A waitlist endpoint taking party size and a name through a record DTO with Bean Validation (`@Valid`, `@NotBlank`, `@Size`, `@Min`, `@Max`, `@Pattern`), answering 201 through `ResponseEntity` — and separating a malformed request (400 with field detail) from a party size no table in the restaurant could ever seat (400).
steps.follows: The floor is readable; this is the first thing that changes it, so validation belongs here.

story.want: add a party to the waitlist by size and name
story.so: the list survives the evening better than a marker pen does

steps.summary: A party joins the waitlist by name and covers and gets an id back; a size no table could seat is refused differently from a malformed body.

codes: the body fails validation; `errors[]` names each field
no table in this branch could ever seat that many; `maxCovers` says the largest
the party is not on this branch's list

data: parties(id, branch_id, name, covers, phone, state waiting|seated|left|cleared, joined_at, position)
rules: `name` 1–60 chars, `covers` integer 1–20, `phone` optional E.164 — violations are the validation status with `errors[]`.
`covers` larger than the largest table in the branch (6) is a valid body but an impossible request: 400 /errors/party-too-big with `maxCovers`.
`position` is 1 + the number of parties currently waiting in this branch, computed at insert.

The request is a record DTO with Bean Validation (`@Valid`, `@NotBlank`, `@Size`, `@Min`, `@Max`, `@Pattern`); a malformed body and a broken rule both answer 400 and are told apart by `type` in the body, tested separately. Each entry of `errors[]` is `{field, message}`; a value Jackson cannot read (covers "six") is still a 400 whose `errors[]` names the field. `joinedAt` is read from a `java.time.Clock` bean, never the system time: the grader puts its own `Clock` in its place.
ac_user: they get a number and a place in the queue
she is told nothing here seats nine, and the largest table is six
the form tells her which field is wrong
ac_api: 201 with partyId, position and a Location header; the row is state waiting
done: Endpoint with all three responses; the party row is written; validation and impossible-size are separate types with tests.

try.do: Add the Kulkarnis, six covers. Then add a party of nine. Then submit with the name blank.
try.see: W001 at position 1 with a `Location: /parties/W001` header. Nine is a valid body but an impossible request: 400 party-too-big with `maxCovers: 6` and no row written. A blank name is also a 400, but typed /errors/validation with `errors[]` naming `name` — the `type` tells the two refusals apart.

steps.title: The wait you quote, and the wait they actually have
steps.scene: Meera says forty minutes. It is the number that decides whether the Kulkarnis stay or walk. Nobody has ever checked it against what happened.
steps.build: Quote a wait when the party joins, and measure the real one against an injected `Clock` bean — so both numbers are stored on the entry and a test can move time instead of waiting for it.
steps.follows: A party is on the list. The quote is the promise this whole project is judged on, and the injected `Clock` bean is what makes every time rule testable.

story.want: be quoted a wait when I join the list, and have the real one recorded
story.so: I can decide whether to stay, and the restaurant can check whether the quote was honest

steps.summary: Every party is quoted a wait when they join and the real wait is measured at seating, both from an injected clock.

codes: the party is not on this branch's list

data: parties gains quoted_minutes, quoted_at, waited_minutes nullable; settings DEFAULT_QUOTE_MINUTES (40)
rules: Here the quote is DEFAULT_QUOTE_MINUTES; it is stored on the party with the clock's `now`.
`waitedMinutes` = seatedAt − joinedAt, rounded down, computed from the injected clock at seating and stored — never recomputed on read.
The clock is a `java.time.Clock` bean injected by constructor; tests supply `Clock.fixed(...)`.
The service takes `Clock` (and the repository) by constructor injection — no field injection, no `Instant.now()` outside the clock — so a test constructs it with `Clock.fixed`.
ac_user: it shows the wait they were told
he sees both numbers side by side
ac_api: 201 with quotedMinutes equal to the setting and quotedAt equal to the fixed clock
the clock moved 47 minutes then the party is seated
a later read after the clock moves again
done: Quote stored at join; real wait stored at seating; both under a fixed clock in tests.

try.do: Add a party and read the green panel; click its id to open the party. (The real wait needs time to pass — the tests move the clock 47 minutes and seat them.)
try.see: `quoted 40 min` stamped at join from the settings and the injected `Clock` bean. When the party is seated, `waitedMinutes` is stamped once from the same clock and never recomputed: the party card reads 'quoted 40 min · waited 47 min' however late you open it. A test swaps the `Clock` for a fixed one instead of waiting.

steps.title: Three ways to say no
steps.scene: A new host tries to seat the Kulkarnis at a four-top, then tries to seat a party that is already eating, then tries to seat anyone at table 12, which Joseph has not cleared.
steps.build: Three refusals with three codes: a table too small for the party, a party already seated, a table not yet cleared — thrown from a `@Service` and mapped by `@RestControllerAdvice`, never handled in a controller.
steps.follows: The happy path is built. What a host may not do is the real content of a floor system, and these three become the first rows of its rule table.

story.want: be refused when I seat a party at a table too small, twice, or at an uncleared one
story.so: a mistake at the stand is caught before the guests are walked over

steps.summary: Seating a party can be refused three ways, each with its own type and status, raised from the service and mapped once.

codes: the table has fewer seats than the party has covers
the party is already at a table
the last party has left but the table has not been cleared
the party is not on this branch's list
no such table in this branch

data: seatings(id, branch_id, party_id, table_id, seated_at, left_at nullable, cleared_at nullable, turn_minutes nullable)
rules: Domain refusals are exceptions raised in the service (TableTooSmall, AlreadySeated, TableNotCleared) — never HTTP responses built in a route.
One exception handler maps each to status + type; the mapping table is the single source of truth.
Order of checks: party exists → table exists → party not already seated → table cleared → table fits. The first failure wins, so a test can target each.

Exceptions are thrown from a `@Service` and mapped once in a `@RestControllerAdvice`; no `try/catch` that builds a response inside a controller. A `@WebMvcTest` on the seating controller, with the service replaced by a `@MockitoBean`, proves the mapping without starting the database.
ac_user: refused: the table is too small
ac_api: table with leftAt set and clearedAt null
body has exactly type, title, status, detail, instance and named fields; no stack trace
done: Three refusals from the service, one handler, a test per refusal, and no controller throws `ResponseStatusException` or builds an error `ResponseEntity` for a domain rule.

try.do: Read 'When the floor says no'. Then on the floor click T11 and seat a party of six there; seat an already seated party at a free table; and seat someone at a table whose party has left but which nobody cleared.
try.see: 409 table-too-small, 409 already-seated, 409 table-not-cleared — each its own type, thrown from the seating `@Service` and mapped by the one `@RestControllerAdvice`; the wire panel shows the last ProblemDetail. The checks run in a fixed order (party, table, already seated, cleared, fits) so each refusal can be reached on its own. No controller builds an error response.

steps.title: The table turns
steps.scene: The Kulkarnis leave at 9:20. Joseph clears the table at 9:26. Ravi's question is how long the table was theirs, because that is what turn time means.
steps.build: Clearing a seating stamps how long the party sat, frees the table, and does both inside one `@Transactional` boundary — so the floor never shows a table free while a seating is still open on it.
steps.follows: The clock is started; this is the only ticket that stops it. Until now the floor fills and never empties.

story.want: have clearing a table record how long the party sat and free the table
story.so: turn time is measured rather than estimated at the end of the night

steps.summary: A party leaves and the server clears the table: turn time is stamped and the table freed, in one transaction.

codes: the party has left; the table is now `uncleared`

data: seatings.left_at, cleared_at, turn_minutes (left_at − seated_at); tables.current_seating_id cleared and tables.cleared_at set on clear; parties.state → left then cleared
rules: Turn time is seatedAt → leftAt (what the table earned), not → clearedAt (what the server took).
Clear updates the seating, the table and the party in one transaction; the floor can never show a free table with an open seating.
Leave and clear are each idempotent by refusal: a second call is 409, not a second stamp.
The close is one `@Transactional` service method; the test injects a failure after the first write and asserts nothing persisted.
ac_user: the table is free and Ravi sees the table was theirs for 83 minutes, not 89
ac_api: POST /leave then /clear with the clock moved
turnMinutes equals leftAt − seatedAt; table current_seating_id null
a failure injected after the seating update
rolled back: seating still open, the table still uncleared, the party still left
done: Both endpoints, atomic clear, turn stamped, idempotent by refusal, tested.

try.do: Click a seated table and press Leave; click it again (now grey) and press Clear. Then open the party from the table.
try.see: After Leave the table shows uncleared — not free — because Joseph has not wiped it. After Clear the table is free and the answer carries `turnMinutes`: seated → left, what the table earned, not seated → cleared. Seating, table and party change inside one `@Transactional` boundary; a second Leave or Clear is a 409, never a second stamp.

steps.title: A board nobody can wipe
steps.scene: Ravi asks why a party that arrived at 7:10 was seated after one that arrived at 7:40. The board was wiped at nine.
steps.build: An append-only log written through `JdbcClient`: one row per transition — quoted, seated, cleared — written in the same `@Transactional` boundary as the change, never updated and never deleted.
steps.follows: A party's evening is now complete; this is what remembers it, and the log that proves nobody was overtaken.

story.want: see every quote, seating and clear in a record nobody can wipe
story.so: I can answer why one party was seated before another

steps.summary: Every transition is written to an append-only log in the same transaction, readable per party.

codes: the party exists, events in `at` order
the party is not on this branch's list

data: events(id, branch_id, party_id, seating_id nullable, kind joined|quoted|seated|left|cleared|dropped|paged|billed, at, data json) — insert only
no UPDATE/DELETE against events — enforced by a database rule or a repository with no update method, and a test that proves it
rules: Written inside the same transaction as the change it records; a rolled-back seating leaves no `seated` event.
Events carry ids and facts, never the guest's phone number.
The party's `events` are the only history the UI shows.

Event rows are inserted through `JdbcClient` inside the same `@Transactional` boundary as the change they record; the events repository has an insert and a read and nothing else, so nothing can update them.
ac_user: Ravi asks why 7:10 was seated after 7:40
the timelines show exactly when each joined and was seated — nothing was wiped
ac_api: exactly one `seated` event with table and waitedMinutes
no event data contains the number
done: Every transition writes an event in-transaction; immutability enforced and tested; GET returns ordered events.

try.do: Open a party that has been seated, left and cleared.
try.see: The timeline: joined, quoted, seated, left, cleared — one row per transition, inserted through `JdbcClient` in the same transaction as the change, in `at` order. Nothing in the app can update or delete a line. No event carries the guest's phone number.

steps.title: One file becomes an app
steps.scene: Ravi wants the floor on a screen in the kitchen, and a developer he knows offers to build it if there is an API worth reading.
steps.build: Packages by feature for the floor, the waitlist, seatings and parties; one `@RestControllerAdvice` so every refusal has the same shape; tags, summaries and documented errors, so the springdoc Swagger UI is something that developer could work from.
steps.follows: The rules so far have accumulated in one module. The problem+json shape is settled here.

story.want: read one set of API docs where every refusal has the same shape
story.so: the screen can be built without guessing what an error means

steps.summary: Routers for floor, waitlist, seatings and parties, one error shape, and docs the kitchen-screen developer can build against.

codes: every endpoint with summary, tag (tables, waitlist, seatings, parties) and documented error responses
every 4xx in the codes tables appears on the endpoint that can return it

rules: Packages by feature: `table`, `waitlist`, `seating`, `party`, each with controller/service/repository; controllers hold no rules, and services import nothing from the web layer (no `ResponseEntity`, no Spring web or servlet types).
One handler produces every error body including validation and unexpected exceptions (500, generic detail, request id, no trace).
Every endpoint declares its error responses with an example body.
Every endpoint has `@Tag` and `@Operation`, and every refusal it can give an `@ApiResponse` with a problem+json `@ExampleObject`; springdoc builds the Swagger UI from them; controllers hold no rules.
ac_user: she can see every call and every way it refuses, with examples
ac_api: 409 table-too-small, already-seated, table-not-cleared and 404s are documented with problem+json examples
500 problem+json, type `/errors/internal`, generic detail, and a request id, carried in the body as `requestId` and written in the log; no stack trace
done: Modular layout; docs list errors per endpoint; one handler; no route builds its own error.

try.do: Press Send on any endpoint, then open /swagger-ui.html and expand POST /seatings.
try.see: Every endpoint from the live /v3/api-docs with its summary, its tag and every refusal it documents as a problem+json example. Packages by feature (table, waitlist, seating, party), services that import nothing from the web, one `@RestControllerAdvice` for every error shape — including a 500 with a `requestId` and no stack trace.

steps.title: The rule table, and then the rule changes
steps.scene: Ravi decides a party of two may take a four-top — but only when nobody larger is waiting. It sounds small. It touches seating, the quote and fairness at once.
steps.build: A `@ParameterizedTest` table driven from `@CsvFileSource` of every refusal the floor can give, run through MockMvc on the whole app against a fixed `Clock` — then add the four-top rule and watch which rows move.
steps.follows: The refusals exist and time can be moved, so a rule can now be changed with evidence.

story.want: let a two-top take a four-top only when nobody bigger is waiting, and see what moved
story.so: a seating change does not quietly break fairness

steps.summary: A parametrised rule table covers every refusal, and the 'two may take a four-top' rule is added with only its rows moving.
data: settings gains SMALL_PARTY_UPGRADE = never | when_nobody_larger_waits | always
rules: The table: one row per case — fits / too small / already seated / not cleared / party too big / malformed / two at a four-top with nobody larger waiting / two at a four-top with a four waiting. Each row: given, action, expected status, type.

Upgrade rule: a party may be seated at a table with more seats than covers only if no waiting party with more covers than this one could be seated at that table. (`never` and `always` are the other two settings.)

When the setting does not allow a party at a table with more seats than covers, POST /seatings answers 409 /errors/overtaking; when the reason is a larger party waiting (`when_nobody_larger_waits`), `mustSeatFirst` names that party.
`@CsvFileSource`; the test drives the whole app through MockMvc (`@SpringBootTest` with `@AutoConfigureMockMvc`) with a fixed `Clock` bean.
Switching SMALL_PARTY_UPGRADE changes exactly the two upgrade rows.

The table is one `@ParameterizedTest` with `@CsvFileSource`, driven through MockMvc on the whole app (`@SpringBootTest` with `@AutoConfigureMockMvc`, because the rows need the database) with a fixed `Clock` bean; the rule change is a `@TestPropertySource` override.

the Kulkarnis (6) waiting for the only six-top... and a four waiting
she seats a two at a four-top
ac_api: every refusal type appears in at least one row; all pass
only the two upgrade rows change outcome
done: Table exists, parametrised, all rows covered; upgrade rule implemented and its rows isolated; GET /settings.

try.do: Switch 'a smaller party may take a larger table' between the three settings and watch the rule table.
try.see: Exactly the two rows tagged `upgrade` move. Under the default a two takes a four-top only when no waiting party with more covers would fit it — otherwise 409 overtaking with `mustSeatFirst` naming who goes first. These are the rows of src/test/resources/rules.csv that the `@ParameterizedTest` runs through MockMvc on the whole app, on a fixed `Clock`, under each setting; GET /settings shows the live values.

steps.title: It runs on the machine by the till
steps.scene: Ravi has a small PC by the till that runs the billing software. He is not installing Java on it.
steps.build: A Dockerfile that builds the Spring Boot jar in a first stage and runs it on an Eclipse Temurin JRE base, an image built and run with a mapped port, and `server.address` bound to 0.0.0.0 (from `HOST`) so the kitchen screen can reach it.
steps.follows: The app is finished and tested; this is the first day it leaves your laptop.

story.want: run the floor from a single image on the machine by the till
story.so: I do not need a developer to start it

steps.summary: The app builds into an image and runs in a container on the PC by the till, reachable from the kitchen screen.

codes: up and can reach its database

rules: Dockerfile in two stages: the jar is built in a first stage (`eclipse-temurin:21-jdk` running the Maven Wrapper) and copied into `eclipse-temurin:21-jre`; `EXPOSE 8080`, `ENTRYPOINT java -jar app.jar`; `server.address=0.0.0.0`. The machine that builds the image needs Docker and nothing else.
`docker build -t tableturn .` and `docker run -p 8080:8080 tableturn` are the only commands; README shows them.
The kitchen screen (another machine) reaches the floor on the till PC's IP:8080.
ac_user: Ravi, no Python or Java installed
the floor opens on the kitchen screen
done: Image builds; serves on the mapped port from another machine; README has both commands.

try.see: The dot is green only when /actuator/health answers UP, which needs the database. The same floor answers on port 8080 from an `eclipse-temurin:21-jre` container running the jar built in the image's first stage, bound to 0.0.0.0 — reachable from the kitchen screen on the till PC's IP, with no Python or Java installed on it.

steps.title: It survives the nightly power cut
steps.scene: The power goes at 10:40 on a Saturday. The waitlist, and everyone's quoted times, are gone.
steps.build: A volume for the H2 file, configuration through an env-file instead of baked into the image, a .dockerignore, logs to stdout — and the README that walks one party from the door to the bill.
steps.follows: The image ran once; this makes it something Ravi can be handed.

story.want: survive the nightly power cut without losing the waitlist
story.so: nineteen people at the door do not lose their place

steps.summary: Data survives `docker rm`, configuration comes from an env-file, logs go to stdout, and the README walks one party door-to-bill.
data: H2 file on a named volume at /data; DATABASE_URL=jdbc:h2:file:/data/tableturn, mapped to spring.datasource.url
.dockerignore excludes tests, .git, local H2 files and target/ (the jar is built inside the image)
rules: Every setting (DATABASE_URL - the JDBC URL of the H2 file -, DEFAULT_QUOTE_MINUTES, SMALL_PARTY_UPGRADE, HOST, PORT) via `--env-file`; nothing baked in.
Logs to stdout/stderr, one line per event; no file inside the container.
README: build, run with volume + env-file, and the exact curl calls for join → quote → seat → leave → clear.

Settings arrive as environment variables through Spring relaxed binding (`DEFAULT_QUOTE_MINUTES` → `default-quote-minutes`, `SMALL_PARTY_UPGRADE` → `small-party-upgrade`); DATABASE_URL, HOST and PORT are mapped in application.yml; the env-file is the only configuration input; the H2 file lives on the volume.
ac_user: every party and their quoted time are still on the list
he edits one line and restarts
ac_api: docker rm + run with the same volume
every request and event line; nothing written under /app
done: Volume, env-file, .dockerignore, stdout logging, README — each verified.
